chapters.title: Unit 12: The Cat and the Fox

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Glossary

  • Q: Q1. tricks
    Ans: A skilful act performed for entertainment or amusement.
  • Q: Q2. meekly
    Ans: In a quiet, gentle, and obedient manner.
  • Q: Q3. insultingly
    Ans: Causing or intending to cause somebody to feel insulted.
  • Q: Q4. wiles
    Ans: Clever tricks that somebody uses in order to get what they want or make somebody behave in a particular way.
  • Q: Q5. chaser
    Ans: A person / animal who follows somebody / something.
  • Q: Q6. dare
    Ans: To be brave enough to do something.

Comprehension — A. Answer the following questions

  • Q: Q1. Who are the main characters of the story?
    Ans: The main characters are the cat and the fox. The cat is meek and friendly and knows only one trick, while the fox is proud and claims to be the master of a hundred arts and wiles. The story is about their meeting in the jungle and what happens when the hunter's dogs come.
  • Q: Q2. Are there any minor characters in the story? If so who are they?
    Ans: Yes, there are minor characters. They are the cat's friend, who told her that the fox was the cleverest and most intelligent among all the animals in the jungle, the hunter, and his four dogs, who caught the fox.
  • Q: Q3. Why was the fox proud of himself? Explain with reference to the story?
    Ans: The fox was proud because he had a very high opinion of himself. He believed he was the cleverest animal, looked proudly at the cat and could not even decide for a long time whether he should bother to answer her. He boasted, "As for me, I am master of a hundred arts and wiles. Besides that, I have numerous tricks to help me through the dangers I encounter."
  • Q: Q4. How did the cat save herself from the dogs?
    Ans: The cat saved herself by using the only trick she knew. As soon as the hunter came with four dogs, she moved quickly up a tree, sat among the top-most branches and hid herself well in the leaves of the tree, where the dogs could not reach her.
  • Q: Q5. Which character do you dislike and why?
    Ans: I dislike the fox. He is proud and rude. He called the friendly cat a "poor and miserable mouse-chaser" and a "poor fool", laughed at her insultingly and said, "How I pity you!" In the end his pride was useless, because the dogs caught him while his hundred tricks could not save him.
  • Q: Q6. Who is your favourite character in the story and why?
    Ans: My favourite character is the cat. She is polite and meek: she greets the fox in a very friendly way, saying, "Good day, dear Sir Fox, how are you?" She knows only one trick, but she knows it well and uses it at the right moment to save her life. She is satisfied with her one safe way.
  • Q: Q7. What is the setting of the story?
    Ans: The setting is a jungle in olden days. The cat meets the fox there as they walk in the jungle, and the rest of the story happens near a tree in the same jungle, where the cat climbs up and the dogs catch the fox.

options: Clever tricks used to get what somebody wants

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary — A. Find the meaning of the following words in a dictionary and locate entry words

  • Q: Q1. arts
    Ans: Skills or tricks; special ways of doing something. In the story the fox claims to know a hundred arts, that is, a hundred clever tricks.
  • Q: Q2. clever
    Ans: Adjective. Quick to understand, learn and make good judgements; having a good mind. The cat's friend told her that the fox was the cleverest animal in the jungle.
  • Q: Q3. intelligent
    Ans: Adjective. Having a high ability to learn, understand and think logically. The fox was said to be the most intelligent among all the animals in the jungle.
  • Q: Q4. pity
    Ans: A feeling of sadness and sympathy for the suffering of others. The proud fox said to the cat, "How I pity you!" because she knew only one trick.
  • Q: Q5. climb
    Ans: Verb. To go up something high, such as a tree or a mountain, using the hands and feet. The cat's only trick was to climb the tree and save herself.
  • Q: Q6. encounter
    Ans: Verb. To meet or face something, often unexpectedly. The fox said his numerous tricks helped him through the dangers he encountered.

Vocabulary — B. Find three adverbs from the story then change those adverbs into adjectives (Example: adverb — mockingly, adjective — mocking)

  • Q: Q1. Find an adverb from the story and change it into an adjective.
    Ans: Adverb: meekly — Adjective: meek. The cat answered the fox meekly, in a quiet and gentle manner.
  • Q: Q2. Find an adverb from the story and change it into an adjective.
    Ans: Adverb: insultingly — Adjective: insulting. The fox laughed insultingly at the cat's one trick.
  • Q: Q3. Find an adverb from the story and change it into an adjective.
    Ans: Adverb: quickly — Adjective: quick. When the hunter came, the cat moved quickly up a tree.

Vocabulary — C. Choose the correct option

  • Q: Q1. Which sentence is imperative?
    Options: The players were nervous before the game. / When are you going to Peshawar? / Move the chairs into that corner quickly.
    Ans: Move the chairs into that corner quickly.
  • Q: Q2. Which sentence is declarative?
    Options: May I have a clean plate? / I found my keys on the desk. / When will the store open today?
    Ans: I found my keys on the desk.
  • Q: Q3. Which sentence is exclamatory?
    Options: Javaid used a towel to clean his hands. / I was tempted to take the last piece of cake. / Hurray! I won the match.
    Ans: Hurray! I won the match.

Grammar — A. Use commas to separate items

  • Q: Q1. My favourite colours are blue orange yellow red and pink.
    Ans: My favourite colours are blue, orange, yellow, red, and pink.
  • Q: Q2. I have to clean my room walk the dog and take out the garbage.
    Ans: I have to clean my room, walk the dog, and take out the garbage.
  • Q: Q3. The tree is very tall old thick and green..
    Ans: The tree is very tall, old, thick, and green.
  • Q: Q4. During summer vacations we will go to Bahrain Swat Buneer Batgram and Chitral.
    Ans: During summer vacations we will go to Bahrain, Swat, Buneer, Batgram, and Chitral.
  • Q: Q5. Sadaf bought cake biscuits juices fruits and candies for the party.
    Ans: Sadaf bought cake, biscuits, juices, fruits, and candies for the party.

Grammar — B. Use a semicolon or a colon to complete the following sentences

  • Q: Durdana likes fruits ______ however she does not like apples.
    Ans: ;
  • Q: Mix all the ingredients ______ and put the batter in the oven.
    Ans: ;
  • Q: You will need the following ingredients ______ milk, sugar, flour, and eggs.
    Ans: :
  • Q: Asim does not play cricket often ______ although he is very good at it.
    Ans: ;
  • Q: To make mango shake you will need the following items ______ mangoes, sugar, milk and ice.
    Ans: :

mcqs.q: What part of speech is the word 'clever'?
mcqs.why: The vocabulary notes state that 'clever' is an adjective, meaning quick to understand, learn and make good judgements.

mcqs.q: What does the adjective 'intelligent' mean?
options: Having a high ability to learn, understand and think logically
Feeling sadness for the suffering of others

mcqs.why: The vocabulary exercise changes the adverb 'quickly' into the adjective 'quick', as the cat moved quickly up a tree.

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing — In your note books write a story of your own using the following beginning

  • Q: Q1. In your note books write a story of your own using the following beginning: It was a stormy night when Adil and Akram ____________________
    Ans: Model story: It was a stormy night when Adil and Akram were returning home from their uncle's village. The wind was blowing hard, the rain was falling in torrents, and the narrow path between the fields had turned into mud. Suddenly Akram slipped and fell into a ditch full of water. He cried out for help. Adil did not panic. He lay down on the edge of the ditch, held the branch of a tree firmly with one hand and stretched out the other hand to Akram. "Catch my hand and do not be afraid," he said. Akram caught his hand tightly, and Adil pulled him out with all his strength. Both boys were wet and covered with mud, but they were safe. Holding each other's hands, they walked slowly and reached home. Their mother gave them warm milk and dry clothes. That night Adil and Akram learnt that a true friend never leaves his friend alone in trouble, and that courage and presence of mind are worth more than fear and panic.

mcqs.q: The model story begins with the given line about Adil and Akram. What were the two boys doing?
options: They were returning home from their uncle's village
They were going to their uncle's village
They were playing in the fields
They were bathing in a ditch
mcqs.why: The model story says it was a stormy night when Adil and Akram were returning home from their uncle's village.

mcqs.q: What was the weather like on that stormy night in the model story?
options: The wind was blowing hard and the rain was falling in torrents
It was a calm and clear night
mcqs.why: The model story describes the wind blowing hard and the rain falling in torrents on the stormy night.

mcqs.q: What happened to Akram on the narrow path between the fields?
options: He lost his bag in the mud
He slipped and fell into a ditch full of water
He was caught in the heavy rain alone
He climbed a tree for safety
mcqs.why: The model story says the path had turned into mud and Akram slipped and fell into a ditch full of water and cried for help.

mcqs.q: How did Adil save Akram from the ditch?
options: He ran home and brought a rope
He lay down on the edge of the ditch, held a tree branch firmly with one hand and stretched out the other hand
He jumped into the ditch and swam with him
He called the villagers to pull Akram out
mcqs.why: The model story says Adil lay on the edge of the ditch, held a branch firmly with one hand and stretched out the other to Akram.

mcqs.q: What did Adil say to Akram while saving him?
options: 'Catch my hand and do not be afraid.'
mcqs.why: The model story quotes Adil's words to Akram: 'Catch my hand and do not be afraid.'

mcqs.q: How did Adil pull Akram out of the ditch?
options: With the help of a passing farmer
With a long rope tied to a tree
With all his strength, after Akram caught his hand tightly
mcqs.why: The model story says Akram caught Adil's hand tightly and Adil pulled him out with all his strength.

mcqs.q: What was the condition of the two boys after the rescue?
options: They were wet and covered with mud, but they were safe
They were lost in the fields
mcqs.why: The model story says both boys were wet and covered with mud, but they were safe, and they reached home holding hands.

mcqs.q: What did their mother give Adil and Akram when they reached home?
mcqs.why: The model story says their mother gave them warm milk and dry clothes when they reached home.

mcqs.q: What lesson did Adil and Akram learn that night about a true friend?
options: A true friend visits only in good weather
A true friend never leaves his friend alone in trouble
A true friend always carries a rope
A true friend runs home first in danger
mcqs.why: The model story ends with the lesson that a true friend never leaves his friend alone in trouble.

mcqs.q: According to the model story, what is worth more than fear and panic?
mcqs.why: The model story concludes that courage and presence of mind are worth more than fear and panic.

chapters.title: Unit 13: Electricity

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Glossary — Word Meanings

  • Q: Q1. conserve
    Ans: To protect something in the environment from harm, running out or destruction.
  • Q: Q2. appliances
    Ans: A device or piece of equipment designed to perform a specific task; electrical and gas devices.
  • Q: Q3. generated
    Ans: To produce or create.
  • Q: Q4. transmission
    Ans: To cause something to pass on from one place to another.
  • Q: Q5. distribution
    Ans: The way in which something is shared out or spread over an area.
  • Q: Q6. voltage
    Ans: The difference in charge between two points.
  • Q: Q7. geothermal
    Ans: Relating to or produced by the internal heat of the earth.

Comprehension A — Answer the following questions

  • Q: Q1. What is hydroelectricity?
    Ans: Hydroelectricity is the electricity produced from the energy of flowing water. In the lesson, the generators at power stations are driven by water, and the picture shows Tarbela Dam, an earth-filled dam on the Indus River in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where electricity is made from river water.
  • Q: Q2. How does electricity reach different places?
    Ans: Electricity is generated at power stations by generators and travels on the transmission line. It does not come to our houses directly from the transmission grid; it is first moved down to the distribution grid, and this conversion of power happens in a power substation. The distribution wires then carry it to a neighbourhood transformer, which reduces the voltage even more, and finally it passes through a meter into our houses.
  • Q: Q3. Make a list of three ways through which we can save electricity in school.
    Ans: Three ways to save electricity in school are: (1) switch off the fans and tube lights when we leave the classroom; (2) switch off lights and fans when they are not in use; (3) use energy-saving bulbs instead of ordinary bulbs, and put up 'Save Electricity' posters to remind everyone.
  • Q: Q4. Do you know how solar power works? Explain with the help of figure below.
    Ans: Yes. As shown in the figure 'How solar power works', the rays of the sun fall on the solar panels fixed on the roof of the house. The panels change the sunlight into electricity, and this electricity is supplied through wires to run the appliances of the house, such as the fridge, the lamp and the television shown in the figure.

Comprehension B — State whether the following statements are true or false

  • Q: 1. Conversion of power happens in a power substation.
    Ans: True
  • Q: 2. It is safe to plug in the outlet with wet hands.
    Ans: False — It is not safe. We should never touch an outlet or plug in a cord with wet hands, because liquids near electrical devices can give us a shock and we could be seriously injured.
  • Q: 3. Stay away from substations and power lines.
    Ans: True
  • Q: 4. Do climb on power poles.
    Ans: False — We should never climb on power poles; it is very dangerous.
  • Q: 5. Never fly kites near power lines.
    Ans: True

mcqs.q: What does 'conserve' mean in the glossary?
options: To produce or create something new
To protect something in the environment from harm, running out or destruction
To pass something from one place to another
To share something out over an area
mcqs.why: The glossary defines conserve as protecting something in the environment from harm, running out or destruction.

mcqs.q: What are 'appliances'?
options: The difference in charge between two points
A deep narrow valley with steep sides
A device or piece of equipment designed to perform a specific task
mcqs.why: The glossary says appliances are devices or pieces of equipment designed to perform a specific task, such as electrical and gas devices.

mcqs.q: What does 'generated' mean?
mcqs.why: The glossary defines generated as to produce or create, as electricity is generated at power stations.

mcqs.q: What does 'transmission' mean?
options: The way something is shared out over an area
A device for a specific task
To cause something to pass on from one place to another
mcqs.why: The glossary defines transmission as causing something to pass on from one place to another, like electricity on transmission lines.

mcqs.q: What does 'distribution' mean?
options: The way in which something is shared out or spread over an area
A layer formed on top of a liquid
mcqs.why: The glossary defines distribution as the way in which something is shared out or spread over an area.

mcqs.q: What is 'voltage'?
options: The rays of the sun on a panel
The difference in charge between two points
mcqs.why: The glossary defines voltage as the difference in charge between two points, which the transformer reduces.

mcqs.q: What does 'geothermal' mean?
options: Relating to or produced by the internal heat of the earth
Made from the energy of flowing water
mcqs.why: The glossary says geothermal relates to or is produced by the internal heat of the earth.

mcqs.q: What is hydroelectricity?
options: Electricity produced from the internal heat of the earth
Electricity produced from the energy of flowing water
mcqs.why: The notes define hydroelectricity as electricity produced from the energy of flowing water, with generators driven by water.

mcqs.q: Where is Tarbela Dam, mentioned in the lesson?
options: On the Ravi River in Punjab
An earth-filled dam on the Indus River in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
On the roof of a house with solar panels
mcqs.why: The notes say the picture shows Tarbela Dam, an earth-filled dam on the Indus River in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where electricity is made from river water.

mcqs.q: Where does the conversion of power happen?
mcqs.why: The notes state that electricity moves from the transmission grid to the distribution grid and this conversion of power happens in a power substation.

mcqs.q: What does a neighbourhood transformer do in the journey of electricity to our houses?
options: It reduces the voltage even more
It measures the electricity in the house
mcqs.why: The notes say distribution wires carry electricity to a neighbourhood transformer, which reduces the voltage even more before it passes through a meter into houses.

mcqs.q: In solar power, what do the solar panels on the roof do?
options: They reduce the voltage for the house
They carry electricity from the power station
They change the sunlight into electricity
They store water for the dam
mcqs.why: The notes explain that rays of the sun fall on solar panels on the roof and the panels change the sunlight into electricity for house appliances.

mcqs.q: Which is one way to save electricity in school given in the notes?
options: Keep fans running in empty classrooms
Use ordinary bulbs instead of energy-saving bulbs
Switch off the fans and tube lights when we leave the classroom
Leave lights on when they are not in use
mcqs.why: The notes list switching off fans and tube lights when leaving the classroom as a way to save electricity in school.

mcqs.q: What is the correct safety rule about wet hands and outlets?
options: It is safe to plug in an outlet with wet hands
We should never touch an outlet or plug in a cord with wet hands
Wet hands protect us from electric shock
We should use wet hands near electrical devices
mcqs.why: The notes correct the false statement: it is not safe, and we should never touch an outlet or plug in a cord with wet hands because liquids near electrical devices can give a shock.

mcqs.q: Which safety statement is true according to the notes?
options: We should climb on power poles
We should fly kites near power lines
We should stay away from substations and power lines
We should touch power lines carefully
mcqs.why: The notes mark 'Stay away from substations and power lines' as true, and also mark 'Never fly kites near power lines' as true.

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar — Quotation Marks A: Punctuate the following sentences

  • Q: Q1. I got an A on my test said Kiran
    Ans: "I got an A on my test," said Kiran. (Done in the book.)
  • Q: Q2. The leader said we should win the elections
    Ans: The leader said, "We should win the elections."
  • Q: Q3. I would like to go with you Jameel said
    Ans: "I would like to go with you," Jameel said.
  • Q: Q4. I hate you she screamed
    Ans: "I hate you!" she screamed.
  • Q: Q5. can we go to school early he said
    Ans: "Can we go to school early?" he said.

mcqs.q: Which is the correctly punctuated form of: I got an A on my test said Kiran?
options: "I got an A on my test," said Kiran.
I got an A on my test, said Kiran.
"I got an A on my test" said, Kiran
I got "an A on my test," said Kiran.
mcqs.why: The notes give the solved sentence as "I got an A on my test," said Kiran, with quotation marks around the spoken words.

mcqs.q: Which is the correctly punctuated form of: The leader said we should win the elections?
options: The leader said we should "win the elections."
"The leader said, we should win the elections."
The leader said, "We should win the elections."
The leader, said "we should win the elections"
mcqs.why: The notes give: The leader said, "We should win the elections." — the spoken words are inside quotation marks after a comma.

mcqs.q: Which is the correctly punctuated form of: I would like to go with you Jameel said?
options: Jameel said "I would like to go with you."
"I would like to go with you," Jameel said.
I would like to go with you, "Jameel said."
"I would like to go with you" Jameel, said.
mcqs.why: The notes give: "I would like to go with you," Jameel said, with the quote first and a comma inside the closing quotation mark.

mcqs.q: Which is the correctly punctuated form of: I hate you she screamed?
mcqs.why: The notes give: "I hate you!" she screamed, keeping the exclamation mark inside the quotation marks with the shouted words.

mcqs.q: Which is the correctly punctuated form of: can we go to school early he said?
options: "Can we go to school early?" he said.
Can we go to school early? "he said."
"can we go to school early," he said?
He said, can we go to school early?
mcqs.why: The notes give: "Can we go to school early?" he said, with a capital C and the question mark inside the quotation marks.

mcqs.q: In the sentence 'The leader said, "We should win the elections."', where do the quotation marks go?
options: Around the whole sentence including 'The leader said'
Only around the exact words the leader spoke
After the full stop at the end only
mcqs.why: In the solved sentence the quotation marks enclose only the leader's spoken words, 'We should win the elections.', not the reporting words.

mcqs.q: Why does 'We' begin with a capital letter inside the quotation in the leader sentence?
options: Because every word inside quotes is capitalised
Because it is the first word of the spoken sentence
Because it comes after the word 'said' in every case
mcqs.why: The spoken sentence inside the quotation marks begins with a capital W because it is the first word of the quoted sentence: "We should win the elections."

mcqs.q: In '"Can we go to school early?" he said', why is 'Can' capitalised?
options: Because the original unpunctuated sentence was all lower case
Because it begins the quoted question
Because questions never use capital letters
mcqs.why: The notes capitalise Can because it is the first word of the quoted question, even though the unpunctuated sentence began with lower-case 'can'.

mcqs.q: In '"I got an A on my test," said Kiran', where is the comma placed?
options: Inside the closing quotation mark, at the end of the spoken words
mcqs.why: The solved sentence places the comma inside the closing quotation mark at the end of the spoken words, before 'said Kiran'.

mcqs.q: In '"I hate you!" she screamed', what punctuation ends the spoken words?
options: A comma inside the quotation marks
A full stop after the quotation marks

Writing — Composition: 'Uses of Electricity in our Daily Life'

  • Q: Q1. Write a composition of three or more paragraphs following conventions of essay writing on the 'Uses of Electricity in our Daily Life' with the help of the mind map.
    Ans: Electricity is one of the greatest wonders of science, and modern life is not possible without it. It is the most versatile energy source that we have, and we have been using it in homes and businesses for more than a hundred years. From morning till night, almost everything we do depends on electricity in one way or another. Electricity gives us light, heating and cooling in our daily life. Electric lamps and bulbs light our homes, schools and streets, while electric heaters keep us warm in winter and fans cool us in summer. It also gives us motion and power: machines in factories work with electricity, and appliances such as washing machines and electric cookers make our housework easy. Electricity is also a great means of communication and entertainment, because computers and televisions run on it. In short, electricity has played a vital part in our past and, if we conserve it, it could play a different and even better role in our future. We should use it carefully, switch off lights and fans when they are not needed, and never waste this precious energy.

chapters.title: Unit 14: The Stream Where I Played

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Glossary — Word Meanings

  • Q: Q1. ravine
    Ans: A deep narrow valley with steep sides.
  • Q: Q2. endless
    Ans: Never finishing, or seeming never to finish.
  • Q: Q3. scummy
    Ans: A layer of unpleasant or unwanted material that has formed on the top of a liquid.
  • Q: Q4. foul
    Ans: Extremely unpleasant.
  • Q: Q5. decayed
    Ans: To (cause something to) become gradually damaged, worse, or less.
  • Q: Q6. fade
    Ans: To (cause to) lose colour, brightness, or strength gradually.

Comprehension A — Answer the following questions

  • Q: Q1. How do litter and pollution affect plants and animals?
    Ans: Litter and pollution make the water of streams and rivers dirty and scummy and make the land foul and decayed, as happened to the stream in the poem. Plants and animals living in and around such water lose their clean home, because people cannot survive — and neither can plants and animals — without clean air, water and land.
  • Q: Q2. Make a list of possible ways to help stop pollution.
    Ans: We can help stop pollution in these ways: (1) do not throw garbage into the lakes and streams; (2) walk or ride bikes instead of using cars for short distances; (3) do not dump wastes from homes or factories into oceans, lakes or rivers; (4) recycle things instead of littering; (5) plant more trees; and (6) conserve water.
  • Q: Q3. Discuss some causes of pollution.
    Ans: The main causes of pollution are: burning fossil fuels in cars and trucks, which pollutes the air; dumping wastes from homes and factories into oceans, lakes and rivers, which causes water pollution; spilling chemicals in rivers and oil spills in the oceans; and littering, which contributes to soil pollution.
  • Q: Q4. Has the city / village where you live changed over the years? What changes do you observe? Ask your parents how it has changed over the past decade.
    Ans: Model answer: Yes, the village where I live has changed a lot over the years. There are more houses, shops and vehicles now, and many trees have been cut down. The stream that was once clean has become dirty because people throw garbage into it. My parents tell me that a decade ago the air was fresh, the water was clear and clean, and there were green fields and trees everywhere, just like the stream in the poem.
  • Q: Q5. How many stanzas are there in the poem?
    Ans: There are two stanzas in the poem. In the first stanza the poet remembers the clean stream of his childhood, and in the second stanza he describes how dirty and foul the same stream has become now.
  • Q: Q6. Write the main idea of the poem.
    Ans: The main idea of the poem is that our recklessness and ignorance have completely defaced the world for future generations. The stream where the poet played as a child was once clear and clean, but now it is too dirty even for his own child to play in.
  • Q: Q7. Who is the speaker in the poem?
    Ans: The speaker is the poet himself. He is a grown-up man who played in this stream as a child, and now he sadly sees that the same stream is too dirty for his child.

Comprehension B — Choose the correct answer

  • Q: Q1. Which of the following add to air pollution?
    Options: burning fossil fuels in cars and trucks / spilling chemicals in rivers / oil spills in the oceans / pressure horns
    Ans: burning fossil fuels in cars and trucks
  • Q: Q2. What happens when people dump wastes from homes or factories into oceans, lakes, or rivers?
    Options: it does not flow to other parts of the world / it is food for animals and plants living there / it causes water pollution / it causes air pollution
    Ans: it causes water pollution
  • Q: Q3. What does contribute to soil pollution?
    Options: littering / recycling / conserving / planting trees
    Ans: littering
  • Q: Q4. Why is it important to conserve water?
    Options: we all need it to survive / its nice to drink on a hot day / we need it to swim / animals and plants live there
    Ans: we all need it to survive

We should walk or ride bikes for short distances instead of using cars and trucks, so that less fossil fuel is burnt and the air stays clean. chapters.title: Unit 15: The Man and His Camel

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Comprehension A — Answer the following questions:

  • Q: Q1. What is the author's purpose of writing this story?
    Ans: The author's purpose is to teach a moral lesson: "Give someone an inch and they'll take a mile." The story warns us to be careful before we extend our hospitality to guests, because they can take undue advantage of our generosity and kindness, just as the camel took over the whole tent.
  • Q: Q2. Who are the main characters of the story?
    Ans: There are two main characters in the story: the man, who is the kind and compassionate master, and his camel, who keeps asking for more and more room inside the tent and finally pushes his master out.
  • Q: Q3. Which character do you like and why?
    Ans: I like the man, the master, because he is kind, generous and compassionate. He took pity on his poor camel in the freezing cold and agreed to every request. However, his example also teaches us that we should be careful, because too much kindness can be misused by others.
  • Q: Q4. Keeping in mind the implied meaning of the story, what bad habits can take over our personality?
    Ans: The implied meaning of the story is that when we let things slip into our lives, such as bad habits and negative elements, they often take over and leave us only the worse. Small bad habits, allowed little by little like the camel entering the tent, can grow, take over our whole personality and push out our good qualities.
  • Q: Q5. What is the setting of the story?
    Ans: The story is set in a desert on a cold winter night. A man crossing the desert fixed his tent there and lay down to rest inside it, while his camel was tied outside in the freezing cold.

Vocabulary A — Use dictionary to choose appropriate word definition and identify part of speech of the word.

  • Q: Q1. compassionate — meaning and part of speech
    Ans: Meaning: feeling or showing sympathy and concern for others; kind-hearted. Part of speech: Adjective. In the story the master is called compassionate because he felt pity for his camel in the cold.
  • Q: Q2. struggled — meaning and part of speech
    Ans: Meaning: tried very hard; made a great effort against difficulty. Part of speech: Verb (past tense of struggle). In the story the man and the camel struggled to remain inside the overcrowded tent.
  • Q: Q3. comfortably — meaning and part of speech
    Ans: Meaning: in a comfortable and relaxed way, without pain or worry. Part of speech: Adverb. In the story the camel slept comfortably in the warm tent.
  • Q: Q4. shivered — meaning and part of speech
    Ans: Meaning: shook or trembled with cold or fear. Part of speech: Verb (past tense of shiver). In the story the master shivered outside in the freezing cold.

Vocabulary B — Find and underline the direct quotations enclosed in quotation marks from the text.

  • Q: Q1. Direct quotation — the man's words when the camel peeped inside the tent
    Ans: "What is it?" the man asked.
  • Q: Q2. Direct quotation — the camel's first request
    Ans: "Master, it is very cold outside. Please allow me to put my head inside your tent," the Camel said.
  • Q: Q3. Direct quotation — the man's reply to the camel's first request
    Ans: "Okay, put your head inside the tent," the man said to his camel.
  • Q: Q4. Direct quotation — the camel's second request
    Ans: "Master, my neck feels very cold. Please let me put my neck inside your tent as well."

Grammar A — Change the following direct sentences into indirect.

  • Q: Q1. Saad said, "I'm washing the dishes."
    Ans: Saad said that he was washing the dishes.
  • Q: Q2. Pervaiz announced, "I've broken my left arm."
    Ans: Pervaiz announced that he had broken his left arm.
  • Q: Q3. The fortune teller said, "You will find a good job soon."
    Ans: The fortune teller said that I would find a good job soon.
  • Q: Q4. My brother said, "It's snowing now."
    Ans: My brother said that it was snowing then.
  • Q: Q5. "This is my first trophy," Sultana said.
    Ans: Sultana said that that was her first trophy.

Revision unit 11-15 A — Identify the simple present tense / simple past tense / simple future tense verbs in the sentences below. Write at the end of the sentence whether the verb is in simple present tense / simple past tense / simple future tense.

  • Q: Q1. Hassan ran to the other side of the field.
    Ans: Verb: ran — Simple past tense.
  • Q: Q2. I open the lid of the container.
    Ans: Verb: open — Simple present tense.
  • Q: Q3. The girls will play with each other on the weekend.
    Ans: Verb: will play — Simple future tense.
  • Q: Q4. Waseem swam late into the night.
    Ans: Verb: swam — Simple past tense.
  • Q: Q5. The dog will wag its tail for food.
    Ans: Verb: will wag — Simple future tense.
  • Q: Q6. My dad waters the lawn in the afternoon.
    Ans: Verb: waters — Simple present tense.
  • Q: Q7. The students will study for the final exam.
    Ans: Verb: will study — Simple future tense.
  • Q: Q8. The campers crept towards the open tent.
    Ans: Verb: crept — Simple past tense.
  • Q: Q9. He eats his breakfast early in the morning.
    Ans: Verb: eats — Simple present tense.
  • Q: Q10. My mother will pick me up from school.
    Ans: Verb: will pick — Simple future tense.

Revision unit 11-15 B — Choose the correct option of each of the sentences below.

  • Q: Q1. Ashraf ______ here from Dera Ismail Khan last year.
    Options: moved / moves / will move
    Ans: moved
  • Q: Q2. By tomorrow I ______ 100 pages of the book.
    Options: read / reading / will read
    Ans: will read
  • Q: Q3. They ______ in Mansehra.
    Options: are living / lives / will live
    Ans: are living
  • Q: Q4. She ______ to a movie tomorrow night.
    Options: goes / is going / gone
    Ans: is going
  • Q: Q5. While he ______ for the bus, it rained.
    Options: is waiting / was waiting / will be waiting
    Ans: was waiting

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing — Write a story with the help of pictures strips and speech bubbles.

  • Q: Q1. Write a story with the help of pictures strips and speech bubbles. (Speech bubbles: "Please give me a small branch; I need a handle for my axe." — "The tree was good-natured and gave him one of its branches." — "No sooner had the woodcutter fitted a new handle to his axe from the branch, he began to work on cutting down tree after tree." — "My kindness was misplaced. I suffer for my own foolishness.")
    Ans: The Kind Tree and the Woodcutter: Once a woodcutter came to a big tree and said, "Please give me a small branch; I need a handle for my axe." The tree was good-natured, so it gave him one of its branches. The woodcutter fitted a new handle to his axe from the branch. No sooner had he done this than he began to work on cutting down tree after tree in the forest. At last he started cutting the same kind tree that had helped him. The poor tree said sadly, "My kindness was misplaced. I suffer for my own foolishness." Moral: We should be careful about whom we help, because an ungrateful person can use our own kindness against us.

mcqs.why: The story written from the picture strips and speech bubbles is titled 'The Kind Tree and the Woodcutter'.

chapters.title: Unit 16: Hazards of Smoking

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Comprehension A — Answer the following questions:

  • Q: Q1. How is smoking dangerous for health?
    Ans: Smoking is dangerous for health because it causes serious diseases such as cancer, heart diseases and lung diseases. Years of smoking make the whole body poisonous from within, and after surgery a smoker's skin does not heal as quickly as that of a non-smoker. It also makes the blood circulation irregular in the body, and in the end smoking kills.
  • Q: Q2. What does "to be addicted to something" mean?
    Ans: "To be addicted to something" means to be unable to stop taking or doing something harmful, even when one wants to stop. A person who is addicted to smoking feels a strong need to smoke again and again, just as smokers like Adil start smoking when they are very young and then cannot leave the habit.
  • Q: Q3. How can you help some one stop smoking?
    Ans: We can help someone stop smoking by talking to him kindly and telling him about the dangers of smoking, as Mrs. Aziz advised Mrs. Rasheed. We should explain how smoking causes cancer, heart and lung diseases, how it badly affects his performance in school and his appearance, and advise him to spend less time with friends who smoke, so that he is convinced to quit smoking.
  • Q: Q4. What should you do if someone offers you a cigarette?
    Ans: If someone offers me a cigarette, I should politely refuse and say "No, thank you." I should remember that young boys only think it is cool to smoke cigarettes, but in fact smoking is not cool; smoking is injurious to health and it kills, so I must never accept it.
  • Q: Q5. Why aren't people allowed to smoke cigarettes in places like schools, hospitals, restaurants, and stores?
    Ans: People are not allowed to smoke cigarettes in places like schools, hospitals, restaurants and stores because the smoke harms not only the smoker but also the other people present there. Children, patients and other non-smokers inhale the smoke and can fall ill, so smoking is banned in such public places to protect everyone's health.

options: cancer, heart diseases and lung diseases
mcqs.why: The notes say smoking is dangerous because it causes serious diseases such as cancer, heart diseases and lung diseases.

They make the blood circulation regular

mcqs.why: The notes say years of smoking make the whole body poisonous from within, and in the end smoking kills.

does not heal as quickly as that of a non-smoker
mcqs.why: The notes state that after surgery a smoker's skin does not heal as quickly as that of a non-smoker.

options: It makes the blood circulation irregular

mcqs.why: The notes advise that a smoker should spend less time with friends who smoke, so that he is convinced to quit smoking.

options: Take it and hide it in your bag

mcqs.why: The notes say that if someone offers a cigarette, we should politely refuse and say, 'No, thank you.'

mcqs.why: The notes say smoking is banned in such places because the smoke harms others too, and children and patients inhale it and can fall ill.

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary — Use a dictionary to find the meaning of the following words. Also use the words in sentences of your own.

  • Q: Q1. performance — meaning and sentence
    Ans: Meaning: the way in which someone does something, especially how well or badly he does it. Sentence: Smoking badly affects a student's performance in school, so Adil's school performance went down day by day.
  • Q: Q2. appearance — meaning and sentence
    Ans: Meaning: the way a person or thing looks outwardly. Sentence: Smoking spoils a person's appearance, because it changes the skin colour and makes the teeth turn yellow.
  • Q: Q3. prematurely — meaning and sentence
    Ans: Meaning: before the proper or expected time; too early. Sentence: A smoker grows old prematurely and gets wrinkles earlier in life.
  • Q: Q4. wrinkles — meaning and sentence
    Ans: Meaning: small lines or folds in the skin, especially on the face, that appear as a person grows older. Sentence: Smoking leads to wrinkles earlier in life, so a young smoker soon begins to look old.

Grammar A — Rewrite the sentences into the passive voice:

  • Q: Q1. Amir changed the flat tyre.
    Ans: The flat tyre was changed by Amir.
  • Q: Q2. Ayesha read a novel.
    Ans: A novel was read by Ayesha.
  • Q: Q3. I will clean the kitchen.
    Ans: The kitchen will be cleaned by me.
  • Q: Q4. Tahir painted the house.
    Ans: The house was painted by Tahir.
  • Q: Q5. Adnan is playing football.
    Ans: Football is being played by Adnan.

Grammar D — Write short notices in passive voice for each of the pictures below.

  • Q: Q1. Write a short notice in passive voice for the picture: No Smoking sign.
    Ans: Notice (passive voice): Smoking is strictly prohibited here. Cigarettes are not allowed in this area, as smoking is injurious to health.
  • Q: Q2. Write a short notice in passive voice for the picture: No Vehicles / No Parking sign.
    Ans: Notice (passive voice): Vehicles are not allowed here. Parking is strictly prohibited in this area.
  • Q: Q3. Write a short notice in passive voice for the picture: Children playing in a playground.
    Ans: Notice (passive voice): This playground is reserved for children. Children are requested to play only in the playground, and the playthings are to be used with care.

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing — Write a letter to your younger brother who is in hostel, advising him give up smoking and pay heed to studies.

  • Q: Q1. Write a letter to your younger brother who is in hostel, advising him give up smoking and pay heed to studies.
    Ans: Examination Hall, Peshawar. 15th February, 2026. Dear Brother, Assalam-o-Alaikum! I hope you are well in the hostel and busy with your studies. I am writing this letter because I have come to know that you have started smoking in the company of some bad friends. It makes me very sad. Dear brother, smoking is injurious to health and it kills. It causes serious diseases like cancer, heart diseases and lung diseases, and years of smoking make the whole body poisonous from within. It will also spoil your appearance: your skin colour will change, your teeth will turn yellow, you will grow old before time and get wrinkles earlier in life. Your clothes and breath will smell foul, and your performance in school will also fall. Please give up smoking at once and spend less time with friends who smoke. Instead, pay full heed to your studies, for only education can make your future bright. Our parents have high hopes from you. Convey my regards to your friends. I hope you will act upon my advice. Your loving elder brother, Ali

chapters.title: Unit 17: The Qissa Khwani Bazaar

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Comprehension A — Answer the following questions:

  • Q: Q1. Why is Qissa Khwani Bazaar called the Bazaar of story tellers?
    Ans: It is called the Bazaar of story-tellers because, centuries ago, merchants and travellers staying in the inns round the bazaar would sit round a fire at night, sipping qahwa and telling stories. There were also professional story-tellers who remembered these stories, made poems (ballads) about them and sang them in the bazaar, so it got the name Qissa Khwani Bazaar, the bazaar of the story-tellers.
  • Q: Q2. Where is Khyber Bazaar?
    Ans: Khyber Bazaar is in Peshawar, near Qissa Khwani Bazaar. As we approach the bazaar from the cantonment side, we first come to the Khyber Bazaar and then to the Qissa Khwani Bazaar.
  • Q: Q3. Why is Qissa Khwani Bazaar called the heart of the main city?
    Ans: Qissa Khwani Bazaar is called the heart of the main city because it stands in the centre of Peshawar and has always been its busy centre of trade. On both sides of its broad road there are all kinds of shops — general merchants, book shops, fruit and flower shops, chemists and copper-ware shops — and hawkers and qahwa stalls, so the life and business of the whole city is gathered here.
  • Q: Q4. What is Qahwa and what is it famous for?
    Ans: Qahwa is the Chinese green tea. It is famous as the famous drink of Peshawar. Lovers of the drink sit for hours on wooden chairs or charpais at the qahwa stalls, sipping qahwa and gossiping, and tourists also like to enjoy qahwa served in China tea-pots with the locals.
  • Q: Q5. What is Bazaar-e-Misgran famous for?
    Ans: Bazaar-e-Misgaran is the copper-ware street of Qissa Khwani Bazaar, and it is famous for its vast variety of copper utensils, from a tumbler to a huge "deg" for cooking rice in large quantities. Its beautifully decorated articles, like vases, bowls and trays of all sizes and shapes, and the surahi and samovar, are specially appreciated by tourists from other countries.
  • Q: Q6. Why did the caravans of merchants bring their goods on camel?
    Ans: The caravans of merchants came from distant lands like Samarkand, Bokhara, Iraq and Syria to sell their goods in Peshawar. For such long journeys they needed animals that could carry heavy loads, so they brought their goods laden on camels, for example silk, diamonds and perfumes, and the city inns round the bazaar used to be full of them.

lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary A — Find the meaning of the following words in a dictionary and use them in your own sentence.

  • Q: Q1. pottery — meaning and sentence
    Ans: Meaning: objects, such as pots, cups and plates, that are made of baked clay. Sentence: In the crockery shops of Qissa Khwani Bazaar, costly china and glassware are displayed side by side with local pottery of pretty colours and designs.
  • Q: Q2. litter — meaning and sentence
    Ans: Meaning: rubbish or waste left scattered in a place. Sentence: We should not throw litter on the roads and footpaths of the bazaar; we should keep our city clean.
  • Q: Q3. enormously — meaning and sentence
    Ans: Meaning: very greatly; to a very large degree. Sentence: The tourists liked the beautifully decorated copper articles of Bazaar-e-Misgaran enormously.
  • Q: Q4. hawker — meaning and sentence
    Ans: Meaning: a person who sells goods by going from place to place or in the street, often calling out. Sentence: On the footpaths of the main bazaar, hawkers sell Swati blankets and caps cheaper than the shops.
  • Q: Q5. laden — meaning and sentence
    Ans: Meaning: heavily loaded or carrying a heavy load. Sentence: In old days, merchants came to Peshawar with their camels laden with silk, diamonds and perfumes.

Vocabulary B — Pick out at least ten verbs from the text and write down their present, past, past participle and present participle forms.

  • Q: Q1. bring (Caravans of merchants and travellers brought goods to sell from distant lands.)
    Ans: Present: bring — Past: brought — Past participle: brought — Present participle: bringing.
  • Q: Q2. sell (After the day's business of buying and selling, these merchants would go to an inn.)
    Ans: Present: sell — Past: sold — Past participle: sold — Present participle: selling.
  • Q: Q3. tell (They would sit here round a fire sipping qahwa and telling stories.)
    Ans: Present: tell — Past: told — Past participle: told — Present participle: telling.
  • Q: Q4. sit (Here one finds lovers of the drink sitting on wooden chairs.)
    Ans: Present: sit — Past: sat — Past participle: sat — Present participle: sitting.
  • Q: Q5. go (These merchants would go to an inn for the night.)
    Ans: Present: go — Past: went — Past participle: gone — Present participle: going.
  • Q: Q6. make (They used to remember these stories and make poems (ballads) about them.)
    Ans: Present: make — Past: made — Past participle: made — Present participle: making.
  • Q: Q7. sing (They would start singing their story poems before the shops opened.)
    Ans: Present: sing — Past: sang — Past participle: sung — Present participle: singing.
  • Q: Q8. gather (Children and even the grown-ups would gather round and listen to them.)
    Ans: Present: gather — Past: gathered — Past participle: gathered — Present participle: gathering.
  • Q: Q9. buy (Here you can buy fresh grapes and sweet melons of Afghanistan.)
    Ans: Present: buy — Past: bought — Past participle: bought — Present participle: buying.
  • Q: Q10. find (On the footpaths of the main bazaar you find hawkers offering many articles.)
    Ans: Present: find — Past: found — Past participle: found — Present participle: finding.

Grammar A — Add parentheses to enclose supplemental information, acronyms and dates or letters and/or numbers in a series. Add or remove any punctuation as needed to use the parentheses correctly. One has been done.

  • Q: Q1. She paid a lot Rs. 3000 for the running shoes.

chapters.title: Unit 18: The Mountain and the Squirrel

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Comprehension A — Answer the following questions

  • Q: Q1. Is the poem in the form of a dialogue? if yes, name the narrator?
    Ans: Yes, the poem is in the form of a dialogue between the mountain and the squirrel. The narrator is the poet, Ralph Waldo Emerson, who introduces the quarrel in the opening lines. After that, the squirrel, called Bun, speaks and gives its reply to the mountain.
  • Q: Q2. What is the main idea of the poem?
    Ans: The main idea of the poem is that size is not everything. Every creature, big or small, has its own place, talent and importance in the world. The mountain is big and carries forests, but the small squirrel is lively and can crack a nut, which the mountain cannot do. So no one is superior or inferior.
  • Q: Q3. Write down the implied and explicit meanings of the poem.
    Ans: Explicit meaning: A big mountain quarrels with a small squirrel, calls it 'Little prig', and the squirrel politely defends itself and its small place in the world. Implied meaning: We should never look down upon anyone who is small, weak or poor. Talents differ from person to person, everything has been wisely placed by the Creator, and pride in one's size or power is wrong.
  • Q: Q4. Describe the character of mountain and squirrel in your words.
    Ans: The mountain is very big and proud of its size. It is rude and insulting, and looks down upon the squirrel by calling it 'Little prig'. The squirrel is small but wise, polite and confident. It does not lose its temper; it answers sensibly, admits the mountain's bigness, and proves that it also has a talent the mountain does not have.
  • Q: Q5. What was the cause of quarrel between the mountain and the squirrel?
    Ans: The quarrel started because the mountain was proud of its towering bigness. It insulted the little squirrel and called it 'Little prig', as if the squirrel was small and useless. The squirrel then replied and justified its existence, which became the quarrel in the poem.
  • Q: Q6. Who is your favourite character in the poem? Why?
    Ans: My favourite character is the squirrel. Although it is very small, it is wise, humble and brave. It answers the proud mountain politely and with strong reasons. It teaches us that a small creature also has worth, because it can crack a nut which even the huge mountain cannot do.
  • Q: Q7. In what ways are you useful to your family and friends?
    Ans: I am useful to my family because I help my mother in small household work, bring things from the shop, look after my younger brothers and sisters and obey my elders. I am useful to my friends because I help them in their studies, share my books and notes with them, and stand by them in times of need.

Comprehension B — Complete the gapped summary

  • Q: This poem is a ______ between the mountain and the squirrel.
    Ans: dialogue
  • Q: The mountain is ______ of its towering bigness and looks down upon the squirrel.
    Ans: proud
  • Q: The ______ justifies its existence.
    Ans: squirrel
  • Q: It says that ______ created this universe in a very orderly way after a good deal of thinking.
    Ans: Allah
  • Q: ______ or small, rich or poor have a distinct quality and a definite place.
    Ans: Big
  • Q: Big or small, rich or ______ have a distinct quality and a definite place.
    Ans: poor
  • Q: None is ______ or inferior.
    Ans: superior

Comprehension C — Decide if each of the statements about the poem is true or false

  • Q: 1. The mountain and the squirrel did not agree with each other.
    Ans: True
  • Q: 2. The mountain insulted the squirrel.
    Ans: True
  • Q: 3. The squirrel doubts that the mountain is big.
    Ans: False — The squirrel does not doubt it; it clearly admits, 'You are doubtless very big.'
  • Q: 4. The squirrel says that it takes a year to make all sorts of things and weather.
    Ans: False — The squirrel says that all sorts of things and weather must be taken in together to make up a year.
  • Q: 5. The squirrel says he is quicker than the mountain.
    Ans: True
  • Q: 6. The squirrel is grateful to the mountain for giving him a path to move along.
    Ans: True
  • Q: 7. The squirrel says the mountain is wise.
    Ans: False — The squirrel says that all things are 'well and wisely put' by the Creator; it does not call the mountain wise.
  • Q: 8. The mountain has got many trees on it.
    Ans: True
  • Q: 9. The squirrel cannot crack a nut.
    Ans: False — The squirrel can crack a nut; it is the mountain that cannot crack a nut.

mcqs.why: Comprehension B in the notes completes the summary with: The squirrel justifies its existence, after the mountain looks down upon it.

mcqs.q: What is the correct judgement of the statement 'The squirrel doubts that the mountain is big'?

Vocabulary B — Find three rhyming words from the poem and create three more rhyming words from the words found.

  • Q: Q1. Rhyming words for 'squirrel'

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary A — Deduce the meaning of the following words. Confirm your meaning from the dictionary.

  • Q: Q1. quarrel
    Ans: Deduced meaning: a verbal fight, an angry argument. Dictionary meaning: a ground of dispute or complaint; an angry disagreement between people.
  • Q: Q2. weather
    Ans: Deduced meaning: climate, season. Dictionary meaning: the state of the air and atmosphere at a particular time, such as hot, cold, sunny or rainy conditions.
  • Q: Q3. former
    Ans: Deduced meaning: the one said first, here the mountain, which is mentioned first in the poem. Dictionary meaning: having been previously; the first of two things mentioned.
  • Q: Q4. later
    Ans: Deduced meaning: the last mentioned one, here the squirrel. Dictionary meaning: the second of two things mentioned; coming after in time. In the poem the word used is 'latter', meaning the second one mentioned.
  • Q: Q5. deny
    Ans: Deduced meaning: to say no, to refuse to admit. Dictionary meaning: to declare something untrue; to refuse to give or allow something.
  • Q: Q6. differ
    Ans: Deduced meaning: to have different characteristics, to be unlike. Dictionary meaning: to be different, to be unlike or distinct in nature.
  • Q: Q7. wisely
    Ans: Deduced meaning: after great thinking, in a sensible way. Dictionary meaning: in a way that shows sound judgement and good sense.

Vocabulary C — Write down four adjectives from the poem and change them into adverbs.

  • Q: Q1. large (adjective)
    Ans: Adverb: largely. Example from the poem: 'If I'm not so large as you'.
  • Q: Q2. pretty (adjective)
    Ans: Adverb: prettily. Example from the poem: 'you make a very pretty squirrel track'.
  • Q: Q3. wise (adjective)
    Ans: Adverb: wisely. Example from the poem: 'Talents differ; all is well and wisely put'.
  • Q: Q4. spry (adjective)
    Ans: Adverb: spryly. Example from the poem: 'You are not small as I, and not half so spry'.

Vocabulary D — Read the poem thoroughly and underline the similes, if there are any.

  • Q: Q1. Find the similes (comparisons with 'as') in the poem.
    Ans: There are two comparisons with 'as' in the poem: (1) 'If I'm not so large as you' — the squirrel compares its size with the mountain. (2) 'You are not small as I' — the squirrel compares the mountain's size with its own small size.

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing — Rewrite the fable that you discussed in 'Listening and Speaking' with new ending in your notebooks

  • Q: Q1. Rewrite the fable of the lion and the mouse with a new ending.
    Ans: The Lion and the Mouse: Once a lion was sleeping in the jungle. A little mouse ran over his body and woke him up. The lion caught the mouse and was about to kill it. The mouse begged, 'Please let me go. One day I may help you.' The lion laughed but set it free. After some days the lion was caught in a hunter's net. He roared loudly. The little mouse heard him, came running and gnawed the ropes of the net with its sharp teeth until the lion was free. New ending: The lion did not simply go away. He thanked the mouse and said, 'You are small, but you are my true friend.' From that day the lion made the mouse his adviser. The mouse sat on the lion's back and warned him of hunters and traps, and the lion protected the mouse and its family from every danger. They lived together happily all their lives. Moral: No one is too small to be useful, and kindness is never wasted.

mcqs.q: Where was the lion sleeping when the mouse woke him?
mcqs.why: The rewritten fable in the notes begins with a lion sleeping in the jungle when a little mouse ran over his body and woke him.

mcqs.q: How did the little mouse wake the lion?
options: It gnawed a rope near him
mcqs.why: The fable in the notes says the little mouse ran over the sleeping lion's body and woke him up, and the lion caught it.

mcqs.q: What did the mouse beg the lion to do?
options: Let it go, saying one day it may help the lion
Give it food from the jungle
Make it the king of animals
mcqs.why: The fable in the notes has the mouse begging, Please let me go; one day I may help you, and the lion laughed but set it free.

mcqs.q: What did the lion do after hearing the mouse's plea?
options: He killed the mouse at once
He ran away from the mouse
He laughed but set the mouse free
mcqs.why: The fable in the notes says the lion laughed at the mouse's promise but set it free, which made the later rescue possible.

mcqs.q: How was the lion caught after some days?
mcqs.why: The fable in the notes says after some days the lion was caught in a hunter's net and roared loudly for help.

mcqs.q: How did the mouse free the lion from the net?
options: It gnawed the ropes of the net with its sharp teeth
It cut the ropes with a knife
It called other lions to pull the net
It dug a hole under the net
mcqs.why: The fable in the notes says the mouse came running and gnawed the ropes of the net with its sharp teeth until the lion was free.

mcqs.q: In the new ending, what did the lion say to the mouse?
options: You are too small to be useful
You must leave the jungle forever
You are small, but you are my true friend
mcqs.why: The new ending in the notes has the lion thank the mouse and say, You are small, but you are my true friend.

mcqs.q: What position did the lion give the mouse in the new ending?
options: He made the mouse a hunter
He sent the mouse to the mountain
He made the mouse his adviser
He made the mouse guard the net
mcqs.why: The new ending in the notes says the lion made the mouse his adviser, and the mouse warned him of hunters and traps.

mcqs.q: In the new ending, how did the lion and mouse help each other?
options: The mouse warned the lion of hunters and traps, and the lion protected the mouse and its family
The mouse carried the lion on its back
The lion taught the mouse to roar at hunters

mcqs.why: The new ending in the notes says the mouse sat on the lion's back and warned him of danger, while the lion protected the mouse and its family.

mcqs.q: What is the moral of the rewritten fable?
options: Pride in size is always right
No one is too small to be useful, and kindness is never wasted
Small creatures should never help big ones
Kindness brings no return in life
mcqs.why: The fable in the notes ends with the moral: No one is too small to be useful, and kindness is never wasted.

chapters.title: Unit 19: The King and the Farmer

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Comprehension A — Answer the following questions

  • Q: Q1. Where did the king stop?
    Ans: The king stopped by a big farm. He was passing by the farm when he saw an old farmer planting mango trees there, so he stopped and watched him busy in his work.
  • Q: Q2. What was the old farmer doing there?
    Ans: The old farmer was planting mango trees in the big farm. He was busy in his work when the king saw him.
  • Q: Q3. What did the king ask?
    Ans: The king asked the farmer three questions. First he asked, 'Old man, how old are you?' Then he asked how long the farmer thought he would live. Finally he asked when the mango trees would start bearing fruit.
  • Q: Q4. How did the farmer talk to the king?
    Ans: The farmer talked to the king very respectfully and politely. He smiled, pointed towards the sky, and answered every question wisely and humbly, calling the king 'Sir' and 'my lord'.
  • Q: Q5. Was the king impressed by the farmer?
    Ans: Yes, the king was greatly impressed by the farmer. He called him a wise man, said that the farmer had taught him a good lesson and deserved a reward, and gave him his ring as a gift.
  • Q: Q6. What lesson did the king learn?
    Ans: The king learned that working for others is not foolishness. The farmer had eaten the fruit of trees planted by his father and grandfather, so it was fair for him to plant trees for his sons and grandsons. The king learned that the fruit of hard work is always sweet, and a man should do good work even if he may not enjoy its result himself.
  • Q: Q7. What kind of a reward did the farmer receive?
    Ans: The farmer received a ring as a reward. The king took off his ring and gave it to him as his gift, and the farmer accepted it saying that he had already got the fruit of his labour that day.

Comprehension B — Cloze Exercise: Fill in the blanks with words from the text

  • Q: Once a king was passing by a ______ farm.
    Ans: big
  • Q: He saw an old farmer planting ______ trees.
    Ans: mango
  • Q: The king stopped and watched him ______ in work.
    Ans: busy
  • Q: Then he went forward and ______ him, "Old man how old are you?"
    Ans: asked
  • Q: "______ I will be eighty, two months from now," said the old farmer.
    Ans: Sir
  • Q: "Sir I will be eighty, two months from ______ ," said the old farmer.
    Ans: now

mcqs.q: Where did the king stop?
options: At an inn round the bazaar
By a big farm, where he saw an old farmer planting mango trees
By a river outside the city
At the gate of his own palace
mcqs.why: Comprehension A in the notes says the king stopped by a big farm when he saw an old farmer planting mango trees there.

mcqs.q: What was the old farmer doing in the farm?
options: Planting mango trees, busy in his work
mcqs.why: Comprehension A in the notes says the old farmer was planting mango trees in the big farm and was busy in his work.

mcqs.q: What was the king's first question to the farmer?
options: Old man, how old are you?
When will these trees bear fruit?
mcqs.why: Comprehension A in the notes lists the king's first question as Old man, how old are you, before his questions about life and fruit.

mcqs.q: What age did the farmer say he would soon reach?
options: He would be sixty, two months from now
He would be eighty, two years from now
He would be eighty, two months from now
He would be ninety, two months from now
mcqs.why: The cloze exercise in the notes gives the farmer's words: Sir, I will be eighty, two months from now.

mcqs.q: How did the farmer talk to the king?
options: Very respectfully and politely, smiling, calling him Sir and my lord
mcqs.why: Comprehension A in the notes says the farmer talked very respectfully and politely, smiled, pointed to the sky, and called the king Sir and my lord.

mcqs.q: What was the king's final question to the farmer?
options: When the mango trees would start bearing fruit
Who planted the farm's old trees
mcqs.why: Comprehension A in the notes says the king finally asked when the mango trees would start bearing fruit, after asking the farmer's age and how long he would live.

mcqs.q: Was the king impressed by the farmer?
options: No, he called him a fool and left angry
No, he ignored the farmer's answers
Yes, but he gave him no reward or praise
Yes, greatly; he called him a wise man who had taught him a good lesson
mcqs.why: Comprehension A in the notes says the king was greatly impressed, called the farmer a wise man, and said he had taught him a good lesson.

mcqs.q: What reward did the farmer receive from the king?
options: The king's ring, given as a gift
mcqs.why: Comprehension A in the notes says the farmer received a ring: the king took off his ring and gave it to him as his gift and reward.

mcqs.q: What lesson did the king learn from the farmer?
options: Working for others is not foolishness, and the fruit of hard work is always sweet
Old men should not plant trees
A king should never stop at a farm
Planting trees is a waste of time
mcqs.why: Comprehension A in the notes gives the lesson: working for others is not foolishness, and the fruit of hard work is always sweet.

mcqs.q: For whom was the farmer planting the mango trees?
options: Only for himself to eat next year
For his sons and grandsons, as his father and grandfather had planted for him
mcqs.why: Comprehension A in the notes explains the farmer had eaten fruit of trees planted by his father and grandfather, so he planted for his sons and grandsons.

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary A — Use dictionary to choose appropriate word definition and identify part of speech of the following words

  • Q: Q1. fool
    Ans: Meaning: a silly person who acts without thinking and shows poor judgement. Part of speech: Noun. In the story the king says to the farmer, 'You must be a fool.'
  • Q: Q2. respectfully
    Ans: Meaning: in a polite way that shows respect for someone. Part of speech: Adverb. In the story the old man answers the king respectfully.
  • Q: Q3. bearing
    Ans: Meaning: producing or yielding; 'bearing fruit' means starting to produce fruit. Part of speech: Verb (present participle of 'bear'). The king asks when the trees will start bearing fruit.
  • Q: Q4. surprise
    Ans: Meaning: a feeling of wonder or amazement caused by something unexpected. Part of speech: Noun. In the story the old man asks in surprise, 'Fool, my Lord?'
  • Q: Q5. reward
    Ans: Meaning: something given to a person in return for good work, help or a good deed. Part of speech: Noun. In the story the king gives the farmer a ring as a reward.

Vocabulary B — Find and underline the direct quotations enclosed in quotation marks from the text

  • Q: Q1. Direct quotation from the text
    Ans: "Old man, how old are you?" — spoken by the king.
  • Q: Q2. Direct quotation from the text
    Ans: "Sir, I will be eighty, two months from now," — spoken by the old farmer.
  • Q: Q3. Direct quotation from the text
    Ans: "And how long do you think you will live?" — spoken by the king. The farmer replies, "Only Allah knows how long I am to live."
  • Q: Q4. Direct quotation from the text
    Ans: "When will these trees start bearing fruit?" — spoken by the king. The old man replies, "After about fifteen to twenty years."
  • Q: Q5. Direct quotation from the text
    Ans: "That is a long time from now. You must be a fool." and "You are taking so much trouble to plant these trees but you may never eat their fruit." — spoken by the king.
  • Q: Q6. Direct quotation from the text
    Ans: "I enjoyed the fruit of trees planted by my father and his father before him. Is it not fair that I should do the same? I am planting these trees so that my sons and grandsons may eat their fruit." — spoken by the old farmer.
  • Q: Q7. Direct quotation from the text
    Ans: "You are a wise man. You have taught me a good lesson and deserve a reward. Take this ring as my gift to you." — spoken by the king. The farmer replies, "Sir, I have already got the fruit of my labour today."

Grammar A — Complete the Conditional Sentences (Type I) by putting the verbs into the correct form

  • Q: Q1. If you (send) ______ this letter now, she (receive) ______ it tomorrow.
    Ans: If you send this letter now, she will receive it tomorrow.
  • Q: Q2. If I (do) ______ this test, I (improve) ______ my English.
    Ans: If I do this test, I will improve my English.
  • Q: Q3. If I (find) ______ your ring, I (give) ______ it back to you.
    Ans: If I find your ring, I will give it back to you.
  • Q: Q4. Palwasha (go) ______ shopping if she (have) ______ time in the afternoon.
    Ans: Palwasha will go shopping if she has time in the afternoon.
  • Q: Q5. Safdar (go) ______ to London next week if he (get) ______ a cheap flight.
    Ans: Safdar will go to London next week if he gets a cheap flight.

mcqs.why: Vocabulary A in the notes defines reward as something given for good work, help or a good deed, part of speech noun, as the king's ring.

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing — Write five sentences of your own using first conditional form

  • Q: Q1. Write five sentences of your own using first conditional form.
    Ans: 1. If it rains tomorrow, I will stay at home. 2. If I work hard, I will pass my examination. 3. If you eat too much, you will become fat. 4. If we leave early, we will reach the station on time. 5. If she studies regularly, she will improve her English.

mcqs.q: In the model sentence 'If it rains tomorrow, I will stay at home', what will the writer do if it rains?
mcqs.why: The first model sentence in the notes says: If it rains tomorrow, I will stay at home, so the result of rain is staying at home.

mcqs.q: In the model sentences, what will happen if the writer works hard?
mcqs.why: The second model sentence in the notes says: If I work hard, I will pass my examination, linking hard work to passing.

mcqs.q: In the model sentences, what will happen if you eat too much?
options: You will reach the station on time
mcqs.why: The third model sentence in the notes says: If you eat too much, you will become fat, giving the result of eating too much.

mcqs.q: In the model sentences, what will happen if we leave early?
options: We will reach the station on time
mcqs.why: The fourth model sentence in the notes says: If we leave early, we will reach the station on time.

mcqs.q: In the model sentences, what will happen if she studies regularly?
mcqs.why: The fifth model sentence in the notes says: If she studies regularly, she will improve her English.

mcqs.q: What verb form is used in the if-clause of 'If it rains tomorrow'?
mcqs.why: The model sentence uses rains, the present simple, in the if-clause, and will stay in the main clause, the first conditional pattern.

mcqs.q: What verb form is used in the main clause of 'If I work hard, I will pass my examination'?
options: Base verb alone: pass alone with no will
Will plus base verb: will pass
mcqs.why: The model sentence uses will pass in the main clause after the present simple if-clause If I work hard, the first conditional pattern.

mcqs.q: What is the first conditional pattern shown by all five model sentences?
options: If plus past simple, would plus base verb
If plus present simple, will plus base verb
mcqs.why: All five model sentences in the notes follow If plus present simple in the condition and will plus base verb in the result clause.

mcqs.q: In 'If she studies regularly, she will improve her English', what is the if-clause verb?
mcqs.why: The model sentence uses studies, present simple with she, in the if-clause, and will improve in the main clause.

mcqs.q: In 'If we leave early, we will reach the station on time', what is the main-clause verb phrase?
mcqs.why: The model sentence uses leave in the if-clause and will reach as the main-clause verb phrase for the result.
